title: Scammers use AI to impersonate immigration attorneys to dupe immigrants with fake legal services

reading.body:
AI-generated deepfakes and synthetic media enabled criminals to impersonate a real immigration attorney at scale across social platforms. The scammers used fake videos, profiles, and client testimonials to solicit payment for fraudulent legal services from vulnerable immigrants, directing victims to send money through peer-to-peer payment apps. This represents impersonation fraud deployed at the point where victims search for legal help online, where no verification system prevented a sophisticated impostor from claiming professional credentials.

What would have caught this: social media platforms implementing identity verification for accounts offering professional legal services, or systems that flag accounts impersonating real licensed attorneys by cross-referencing bar registries. The scale of the fraud, with thousands of fake profiles across multiple platforms over nearly a year, suggests the deployment lacked automated defenses against coordinated inauthentic behavior or synthetic media.

Whether the scammers used generative AI to create the deepfakes, trained models to optimize targeting, or deployed other AI systems beyond the synthetic videos and profiles is not established.

reports.title: Scammers steal identity of renowned Miami attorney to target immigrants on social media
South Florida immigration attorney says AI scammers are using his identity to target immigrants
Scammers use AI to impersonate immigration attorneys to dupe immigrants with fake legal services
Legal resident loses thousands seeking citizenship to AI immigration attorney

summary:
Angel Leal, a South Florida immigration attorney with over 30 years of experience, has become the target of artificial intelligence scammers who are using deepfake videos and fake social media profiles bearing his likeness to defraud vulnerable immigrants. The criminals create videos offering immigration services Leal never provides, such as US residency assistance for $2,200, and use testimonials from fake former clients to build credibility. Leal discovered the scheme when potential clients began calling his office, though suspicious activity first appeared last October and has significantly worsened over the past three months.

To combat the fraud, Leal's firm hired an anti-piracy company that has successfully removed nearly 6,500 fake profiles across social media platforms, including 3,500 on TikTok, 2,400 on Facebook, and 544 on Instagram. The scammers typically direct people through social media videos to contact phone numbers via WhatsApp, then send phony contracts and request payment through apps like Venmo, Zelle, or Cash App. Leal advises immigrants to verify the identity of anyone offering legal services online and warns against making immediate payments. He plans to contact local and federal authorities this week to investigate the scams' origin.
